title: What is RNA-seq?
text:
RNA-seq is a way to measure which genes are being expressed in a biological sample.
Cells use DNA as the long-term instruction manual, but they do not use every gene all the time. When a gene is active, the cell often makes RNA copies of that gene. RNA-seq lets us sequence those RNA molecules and estimate which genes were active (or inactive), and how strongly, in each sample.
In this tutorial, we are interested in RNA-seq analysis for the frog Staurois parvus.

text:
2 The nf-core/rnaseq workflow
In this tutorial, we use nf-core/rnaseq to process RNA-seq data in a standardized and reproducible way.
The nf-core/rnaseq pipeline can be visualized as a “metro map” of analysis steps. Each stop represents a tool or processing step, and each colored route represents a different analysis path through the pipeline.



nf-core/rnaseq metro map showing preprocessing, alignment, quantification, post-processing, and final quality-control steps.


Source: nf-core/rnaseq version 3.26.0.






Tip



For this tutorial, we are following the default green path: STAR for alignment and Salmon for quantification. There are multiple valid ways to analyze RNA-seq data, but we will focus on this route.

title: What is RNA-seq?
text:
3 What are FASTQ files?
Sequencing machines produce reads. A read is a short sequence from an RNA molecule. These reads are usually stored in FASTQ files.
FASTQ files often come in pairs:
sample1_R1.fastq.gz
sample1_R2.fastq.gz
For paired-end sequencing:

R1 contains the first read from each fragment
R2 contains the second read from each fragment
.gz means the file is compressed

title: What is RNA-seq?
text:
4 What does the pipeline do?
The pipeline takes raw sequencing reads and turns them into quality-control reports, alignments, and expression estimates. These are the major steps shown in the nf-core/rnaseq workflow.

4.1 Pre-processing
These steps clean up and check the raw sequencing reads before alignment or quantification.

Merge re-sequenced FASTQ files with cat
Auto-infer strandedness by subsampling reads and pseudoaligning them with fq and Salmon
Check raw read quality with FastQC
Extract unique molecular identifiers, if present, with UMI-tools
Trim adapters and low-quality sequence with Trim Galore!
Remove genome contaminants with BBSplit
Remove ribosomal RNA with SortMeRNA



4.2 Alignment and quantification
After pre-processing, the pipeline can follow different routes. The route depends on whether you want genome alignment, transcript quantification, or pseudoalignment.
The default route used in this tutorial is:
STAR -> Salmon
Other available routes include:

STAR -> RSEM
HISAT2 -> no quantification
Pseudoalignment and quantification with Salmon or Kallisto

For STAR, the Sentieon implementation can also be chosen if it is available and configured.


4.3 Post-processing
After alignment and quantification, the pipeline organizes and summarizes the mapped reads.

Sort and index alignments with SAMtools
Deduplicate reads using UMIs with UMI-tools, if UMIs are present
Mark duplicate reads with picard MarkDuplicates
Assemble and quantify transcripts with StringTie
Create bigWig coverage files with BEDTools and bedGraphToBigWig



4.4 Contamination screening
The pipeline can optionally screen selected reads for contamination. By default, this is done on unaligned reads.
Optional tools include:

Kraken2 -> Bracken
Sylph



4.5 Quality control and reporting
Quality control helps us decide whether the sequencing and analysis worked well enough to trust the results.
The pipeline performs extensive QC with tools such as:

RSeQC
Qualimap
dupRadar
Preseq
DESeq2
MultiQC
R

The final report summarizes raw read quality, alignment metrics, gene biotypes, sample similarity, and strand-specificity checks.

title: What is RNA-seq?
section: 5 What do we get at the end?
text:
5 What do we get at the end?
The main outputs are:

Quality-control reports
Alignment or mapping summaries
Gene or transcript expression estimates
Pipeline logs and software version information

These outputs help answer questions such as:

Did the sequencing work well?
Are any samples low quality or unusual?
Which genes are expressed in each sample?
Which samples are ready for downstream analysis?

title: What is RNA-seq?
section: 6 What RNA-seq does not tell us by itself
text:
6 What RNA-seq does not tell us by itself
RNA-seq measures RNA abundance, not every part of biology directly. Gene expression can suggest biological patterns, but interpretation depends on experimental design, replication, annotation quality, and downstream statistics.






Note



Good RNA-seq analysis starts before sequencing. Sample design, metadata, replication, and careful record keeping matter just as much as the computational pipeline.

title: Differential Gene Expression Analysis
text:
This analysis contains head and body RNA-seq libraries from one frog clutch. Day-45 tadpoles were collected before the tank treatment period. At day 103, tadpoles were sampled from one control tank and one flutamide tank.
Important limits are built into the analysis and must accompany interpretation:

Treatment is confounded with tank because there is one tank per condition. The treatment-assignment unit is the tank, so tadpoles within a tank are subsamples rather than independent treatment replicates. Results are therefore described as flutamide-tank versus control-tank associations, not definitive causal effects of flutamide.
The experiment is not a complete tissue × treatment × stage factorial: no young flutamide samples exist. Overall treatment effects across stages, treatment-by-stage interactions, and three-way interactions are not estimable.
All tadpoles came from one clutch, so inference is clutch-specific.
Stage comparisons use different animals collected on different days. They combine age/development with any day- or cohort-specific differences.
Only two old-control head libraries exist. Head contrasts and the tissue-by-treatment interaction are consequently fragile.

4 Salmon import with tximport
DESeq2 recommends importing Salmon transcript quantifications with tximport, then constructing the dataset with DESeqDataSetFromTximport(). This retains gene-specific average transcript-length offsets. TPM values are not used for testing.


Code
quant_dir <- "salmon_quant"
tx2gene_file <- "salmon.merged.tx2gene.tsv"
gtf_file <- "complete.genomic.gtf"

files <- file.path(quant_dir, sample_manifest$sample_id, "quant.sf")
names(files) <- sample_manifest$sample_id
stopifnot(all(file.exists(files)))
stopifnot(length(files) == 24L)

tx2gene_raw <- read.delim(
  tx2gene_file,
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE
)
stopifnot(all(c("transcript_id", "gene_id") %in% names(tx2gene_raw)))
tx2gene <- unique(tx2gene_raw[, c("transcript_id", "gene_id")])
stopifnot(!anyNA(tx2gene), !anyDuplicated(tx2gene$transcript_id))

txi <- tximport(
  files,
  type = "salmon",
  tx2gene = tx2gene,
  countsFromAbundance = "no"
)
stopifnot(identical(colnames(txi$counts), sample_manifest$sample_id))

input_checksums <- data.frame(
  file = c(files, tx2gene_file, gtf_file),

names(gene_annotation)[2] <- "gene_name"

gtf <- rtracklayer::import(gtf_file)
gtf_mcols <- mcols(gtf)
stopifnot(all(c("gene_id", "type", "product") %in% names(gtf_mcols)))

gtf_products <- data.frame(
  gene_id = as.character(gtf_mcols$gene_id),
  feature_type = as.character(gtf_mcols$type),
  product = as.character(gtf_mcols$product),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
gtf_products <- subset(
  gtf_products,
  !is.na(gene_id) & gene_id != "" & !is.na(product) & product != ""
)
product_annotation <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(gtf_products, gtf_products$gene_id),
  function(x) {
    preferred <- unique(x$product[x$feature_type %in% c("transcript", "mRNA")])
    products <- if (length(preferred)) preferred else unique(x$product)
    data.frame(
      gene_id = x$gene_id[1],
      product_description = paste(products, collapse = " | "),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
))
rownames(product_annotation) <- NULL
rm(gtf, gtf_mcols, gtf_products)

title: Differential Gene Expression Analysis
text:
6 DESeq2 construction and fit
The observed cell combinations are represented by one group factor. This is the DESeq2 manual’s recommended simple strategy for explicit cell contrasts and avoids a non-estimable full factorial model.


Code
coldata <- sample_manifest
rownames(coldata) <- coldata$sample_id

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromTximport(
  txi,
  colData = coldata,
  design = ~ group
)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(colData(dds)), colnames(dds)))
stopifnot(qr(model.matrix(design(dds), as.data.frame(colData(dds))))$rank ==
            nlevels(dds$group))

mcols(dds)$gene_name <- gene_annotation$gene_name[
  match(rownames(dds), gene_annotation$gene_id)
]
mcols(dds)$product_description <- product_annotation$product_description[
  match(rownames(dds), product_annotation$gene_id)
]

# Intentional information filter: count >=10 in at least 3 libraries.
# Three is stricter than the actual smallest cell (old-control head, n=2).
genes_before_filter <- nrow(dds)
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= 3
dds <- dds[keep, ]
filter_audit <- data.frame(
  genes_before_filter = genes_before_filter,
  genes_after_filter = nrow(dds),
  genes_removed = genes_before_filter - nrow(dds),
  rule = "count >= 10 in at least 3 libraries"
)
write.csv(filter_audit, "DESeq2_results/prefilter_audit.csv", row.names = FALSE)
filter_audit

dds <- DESeq(dds)
resultsNames(dds)

write.csv(as.data.frame(colData(dds)),
          "DESeq2_results/sample_metadata.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(dds, "DESeq2_results/dds_fitted.rds")

7 Quality control

7.1 Library sizes, effective scaling factors, and zero fractions


Code
library_qc <- data.frame(
  sample_id = colnames(dds),
  sample_core = sub("_S[0-9]+_L[0-9]+$", "", colnames(dds)),
  group = dds$group,
  raw_gene_count_sum = colSums(counts(dds)),
  # tximport supplies gene-by-sample normalization factors that combine
  # average transcript-length offsets with library scaling. Their column
  # geometric means provide a sample-level scaling summary for QC only.
  effective_library_scaling = exp(
    colMeans(log(normalizationFactors(dds)))
  ),
  zero_fraction = colMeans(counts(dds) == 0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
write.csv(library_qc, "DESeq2_results/QC/library_size_factor_zero_fraction.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)

library_qc_plot <- ggplot(
  library_qc,
  aes(x = reorder(sample_core, effective_library_scaling),
      y = effective_library_scaling, fill = group)
) +
  geom_col() + coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "tximport/DESeq2 effective library scaling", x = NULL,
       y = "Geometric mean of normalization factors", fill = "Group") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11)
ggsave("DESeq2_results/QC/effective_library_scaling.pdf", library_qc_plot,
       width = 10, height = 7)
library_qc_plot


Small effective library-scaling values are flags for upstream MultiQC review, not automatic exclusion criteria. Because tximport supplies gene-specific length offsets, these summaries must not be described as ordinary DESeq2 size factors.

7.3 VST, PCA, sample distances, and heatmaps
blind=FALSE uses the fitted dispersion trend for biological visualization and does not remove group effects. A second blind=TRUE PCA is included as design-blind sample QA.


Code
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)
vsd_blind <- vst(dds, blind = TRUE)
saveRDS(vsd, "DESeq2_results/vsd.rds")

make_pca <- function(vsd_object, label, filename) {
  mat <- assay(vsd_object)
  vars <- rowVars(mat)
  top <- names(sort(setNames(vars, rownames(mat)), decreasing = TRUE))[
    seq_len(min(500, nrow(mat)))
  ]
  pca <- prcomp(t(mat[top, , drop = FALSE]), scale. = FALSE)
  percent <- 100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)
  pd <- cbind(as.data.frame(pca$x[, 1:2, drop = FALSE]),
              as.data.frame(colData(vsd_object)))
  p <- ggplot(pd, aes(PC1, PC2, color = group, shape = tissue,
                     label = sub("_S[0-9]+_L[0-9]+$", "", sample_id))) +
    geom_point(size = 3.5) +
    geom_text_repel(size = 2.8, max.overlaps = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) +
    labs(title = paste("PCA:", label),
         subtitle = "500 most variable genes",
         x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", percent[1]),
         y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", percent[2]), color = "Group") +
    coord_fixed() + theme_classic(base_size = 11)
  ggsave(filename, p, width = 10, height = 7)
  list(plot = p, data = pd, top = top, variance = vars)
}

title: Differential Gene Expression Analysis
text:
8 Differential-expression functions
The standard Wald result tests LFC = 0. A separate thresholded Wald result formally tests whether |LFC| > 1. Shrunken LFCs are used for ranking and visualization, not to create p-values.


Code
annotate_result <- function(res, dds_object) {
  out <- as.data.frame(res)
  out$gene_id <- rownames(out)
  out$gene_name <- mcols(dds_object)[out$gene_id, "gene_name"]
  out$product_description <- mcols(dds_object)[out$gene_id, "product_description"]
  out
}

run_comparison <- function(dds, numerator, denominator, comparison_name,
                           alpha = 0.05, lfc_threshold = 1) {
  contrast_vector <- c("group", numerator, denominator)
  res <- results(dds, contrast = contrast_vector, alpha = alpha)
  res_threshold <- results(
    dds, contrast = contrast_vector, alpha = alpha,
    lfcThreshold = lfc_threshold, altHypothesis = "greaterAbs"
  )
  res_shrunk <- lfcShrink(
    dds, contrast = contrast_vector, res = res, type = "ashr"
  )

  out <- annotate_result(res, dds)
  out$shrunken_log2FoldChange <- res_shrunk$log2FoldChange
  out$shrunken_lfcSE <- res_shrunk$lfcSE
  out$threshold_stat <- res_threshold$stat
  out$threshold_pvalue <- res_threshold$pvalue
  out$threshold_padj <- res_threshold$padj
  out$standard_FDR_significant <- !is.na(out$padj) & out$padj < alpha
  out$LFC_threshold_FDR_significant <-
    !is.na(out$threshold_padj) & out$threshold_padj < alpha
  out$threshold_direction <- "Not threshold-significant"
  out$threshold_direction[
    out$LFC_threshold_FDR_significant & out$shrunken_log2FoldChange > 0
  ] <- "Higher"
  out$threshold_direction[
    out$LFC_threshold_FDR_significant & out$shrunken_log2FoldChange < 0
  ] <- "Lower"
  out <- out[order(out$threshold_padj, out$padj, out$pvalue, na.last = TRUE), ]

  write.csv(out, file.path("DESeq2_results/DGE",
    paste0(comparison_name, "_DESeq2_results.csv")), row.names = FALSE)

  result_summary <- data.frame(
    comparison = comparison_name,
    numerator = numerator,
    denominator = denominator,
    genes = nrow(out),
    standard_FDR_below_0.05 = sum(out$standard_FDR_significant),
    threshold_test_FDR_below_0.05 = sum(out$LFC_threshold_FDR_significant),
    threshold_higher = sum(out$threshold_direction == "Higher"),
    threshold_lower = sum(out$threshold_direction == "Lower"),
    NA_pvalue = sum(is.na(out$pvalue)),
    NA_padj = sum(is.na(out$padj)),
    independent_filter_threshold = unname(metadata(res)$filterThreshold)
  )

  pdf(file.path("DESeq2_results/QC", paste0(comparison_name, "_MA.pdf")),
      width = 8, height = 6)
  plotMA(res_shrunk, alpha = alpha, ylim = c(-5, 5),
         main = paste(comparison_name, "(ashr LFC)"))
  dev.off()

  plot_data <- out
  plot_data$plot_padj <- ifelse(is.na(plot_data$threshold_padj), 1,
                               pmax(plot_data$threshold_padj,
                                    .Machine$double.xmin))
  labels <- subset(plot_data,
                   LFC_threshold_FDR_significant & !is.na(gene_name) & gene_name != "")
  labels <- head(labels[order(labels$threshold_padj), ], 10)
  volcano <- ggplot(plot_data,
    aes(shrunken_log2FoldChange, -log10(plot_padj), color = threshold_direction)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.65, size = 1.4) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(-lfc_threshold, lfc_threshold),
               linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(alpha), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
    geom_text_repel(data = labels, aes(label = gene_name), size = 3,
                    max.overlaps = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
      "Lower" = "#2C7BB6", "Not threshold-significant" = "grey75",
      "Higher" = "#D7191C"
    )) +
    labs(title = comparison_name,
         subtitle = paste(numerator, "vs", denominator),
         x = "ashr-shrunken log2 fold change",
         y = expression(-log[10]("threshold-test adjusted p-value")),
         caption = paste0("Formal Wald test of |LFC| > ", lfc_threshold,
                          "; FDR < ", alpha), color = NULL) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "top")
  ggsave(file.path("DESeq2_results/volcano",
                   paste0(comparison_name, "_volcano.pdf")),
         volcano, width = 8, height = 7)

  list(res = res, res_threshold = res_threshold, res_shrunk = res_shrunk,
       table = out, summary = result_summary)
}

title: Differential Gene Expression Analysis
text:
10 Relevant-subset sensitivity fits
DESeq2 usually recommends fitting all groups together, but very different groups can influence the shared gene-wise dispersion. Each main contrast is therefore refit using only its two relevant cells.


Code
run_subset_sensitivity <- function(dds_full, full_result, numerator,
                                   denominator, comparison_name) {
  use <- dds_full$group %in% c(numerator, denominator)
  d <- dds_full[, use]
  d$group <- droplevels(d$group)
  design(d) <- ~ group
  d <- DESeq(d)
  sub_res <- results(d, contrast = c("group", numerator, denominator), alpha = 0.05)
  ids <- rownames(full_result)
  sub_lfc <- sub_res$log2FoldChange[match(ids, rownames(sub_res))]
  sub_padj <- sub_res$padj[match(ids, rownames(sub_res))]
  tab <- data.frame(
    gene_id = ids,
    full_log2FC = full_result$log2FoldChange,
    full_padj = full_result$padj,
    subset_log2FC = sub_lfc,
    subset_padj = sub_padj,
    direction_agrees = sign(full_result$log2FoldChange) == sign(sub_lfc)
  )
  finite <- is.finite(tab$full_log2FC) & is.finite(tab$subset_log2FC)
  summary <- data.frame(
    comparison = comparison_name,
    full_samples = ncol(dds_full), subset_samples = ncol(d),
    spearman_LFC = cor(tab$full_log2FC[finite], tab$subset_log2FC[finite],
                       method = "spearman"),
    direction_agreement = mean(tab$direction_agrees[finite], na.rm = TRUE),
    full_FDR_hits = sum(tab$full_padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    subset_FDR_hits = sum(tab$subset_padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    shared_FDR_hits = sum(tab$full_padj < 0.05 & tab$subset_padj < 0.05,
                          na.rm = TRUE)
  )
  write.csv(tab, file.path("DESeq2_results/sensitivity",
    paste0(comparison_name, "_full_vs_subset.csv")), row.names = FALSE)
  summary
}

11 Older-only paired tissue interaction
The interaction is
\[
(\mathrm{flutamide\ tank\ head}-\mathrm{control\ tank\ head})-
(\mathrm{flutamide\ tank\ body}-\mathrm{control\ tank\ body}).
\]
Tadpole fixed effects account for paired head/body libraries. Treatment main effect is absorbed by tadpole; the custom flutamide_head coefficient estimates the difference-in-differences.


Code
dds_old <- dds[, dds$stage == "Old"]
# Use syntactically safe factor levels for stable coefficient names.
dds_old$tadpole <- factor(make.names(as.character(dds_old$tadpole)))
dds_old$tissue <- factor(dds_old$tissue, levels = c("Body", "Head"))

  dds_old$treatment == "Flutamide" & dds_old$tissue == "Head"
)

paired_mm <- model.matrix(design(dds_old), as.data.frame(colData(dds_old)))
stopifnot(qr(paired_mm)$rank == ncol(paired_mm))

pair_table <- with(as.data.frame(colData(dds_old)), table(tadpole, tissue))
complete_pair_ids <- rownames(pair_table)[rowSums(pair_table > 0) == 2]
paired_design_audit <- data.frame(
  old_libraries = ncol(dds_old),
  tadpoles = nlevels(dds_old$tadpole),
  complete_pairs = length(complete_pair_ids),
  control_complete_pairs = sum(grepl("^C", complete_pair_ids)),
  flutamide_complete_pairs = sum(grepl("^F", complete_pair_ids)),
  model_parameters = ncol(paired_mm),
  residual_df = nrow(paired_mm) - qr(paired_mm)$rank
)
write.csv(paired_design_audit,
          "DESeq2_results/DGE/paired_interaction_design_audit.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)

dds_old <- DESeq(dds_old)

stopifnot(length(interaction_name) == 1L)

  dds_old, coef = interaction_name, res = res_interaction, type = "ashr"

  res_interaction_shrunk$log2FoldChange

# Auxiliary component contrasts come from the separate global, unpaired model.

  ar_blockade_head$res$log2FoldChange[
    match(interaction_out$gene_id, rownames(ar_blockade_head$res))

  !is.na(interaction_out$padj) & interaction_out$padj < 0.05

title: Differential Gene Expression Analysis
text:
13 Leave-one-complete-pair-out stability
Each complete head/body pair is omitted in turn. This does not create new experimental replication; it tests whether leading paired-interaction estimates are dominated by one pair.


Code
paired_hit_ids <- rownames(res_interaction)[
  !is.na(res_interaction$padj) & res_interaction$padj < 0.05
]
full_hit_lfc <- res_interaction$log2FoldChange[
  match(paired_hit_ids, rownames(res_interaction))
]
loo_list <- lapply(complete_pair_ids, function(id) {
  d <- dds_old[, dds_old$tadpole != id]
  d$tadpole <- droplevels(d$tadpole)
  design(d) <- ~ tadpole + tissue + flutamide_head
  mm <- model.matrix(design(d), as.data.frame(colData(d)))
  stopifnot(qr(mm)$rank == ncol(mm))
  d <- DESeq(d, quiet = TRUE)
  nm <- grep("flutamide_head", resultsNames(d), value = TRUE)
  r <- results(d, name = nm, alpha = 0.05)
  data.frame(
    omitted_pair = id,
    gene_id = paired_hit_ids,
    full_log2FC = full_hit_lfc,
    leave_one_out_log2FC = r$log2FoldChange[
      match(paired_hit_ids, rownames(r))
    ],
    leave_one_out_padj = r$padj[match(paired_hit_ids, rownames(r))]
  )
})
loo_stability <- do.call(rbind, loo_list)
loo_stability$direction_agrees <- with(
  loo_stability, sign(full_log2FC) == sign(leave_one_out_log2FC)
)
write.csv(loo_stability,
          "DESeq2_results/sensitivity/paired_interaction_leave_one_pair_out.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
loo_summary <- aggregate(
  cbind(direction_agrees, leave_one_out_log2FC) ~ gene_id,
  data = loo_stability,
  FUN = function(x) c(min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
                      median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
                      max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE))
)
loo_summary

title: Differential Gene Expression Analysis
text:
15 Interpretation
A positive interaction means the flutamide-tank association is more positive in head than body; it may arise from stronger head induction, stronger body repression, or both. A negative interaction has the opposite meaning. Interaction sign is not ordinary gene up- or downregulation.
The most defensible interaction candidates are genes with consistent effect directions, stability when individual complete pairs are omitted, and support in both paired and unpaired models. Statistical interaction does not establish direct androgen-receptor regulation and remains confounded with tank.
Suggested reporting language:

At day 103, tadpoles housed in the flutamide tank differed in gene expression from tadpoles housed in the control tank. Because treatment was applied at the tank level with one tank per condition, treatment and tank effects are inseparable and these contrasts are exploratory. The tissue-dependent association was estimated from six complete head–body pairs (two control and four flutamide; paired-model residual df = 4). Candidate genes were evaluated using paired and unpaired interaction models and leave-one-pair-out stability analyses.

title: File Types and File Sizes
text:
RNA-seq analysis creates many files. Some are small text files that describe your samples. Others are large sequencing or alignment files that can use a lot of space.
This page is a gentle introduction to the file types you may see during RNA-seq analysis. You do not need to understand every detail yet. The goal is to become familiar with the names and what they are generally used for.
Before running a pipeline, it helps to recognize which files are raw data, which files describe the reference genome, and which files are results.

This page is a gentle introduction to the file types you may see during RNA-seq analysis. You do not need to understand every detail yet. The goal is to become familiar with the names and what they are generally used for.

title: File Types and File Sizes
text:
3 FASTQ files
FASTQ files are usually the main input for RNA-seq pipelines.
Paired-end data often has two files per sample:
sample1_R1.fastq.gz
sample1_R2.fastq.gz
The file names usually tell you:

The sample name
Whether the file is read 1 (R1) or read 2 (R2)
Whether the file is compressed (.gz)

FASTQ files can be large. A single compressed FASTQ file may be several gigabytes.

title: File Types and File Sizes
text:
4 Reference files
Reference files describe the genome or transcriptome you want to compare your reads against.
Common reference files include:
genome.fa
annotation.gtf
For non-model organisms like Staurois parvus, reference files may come from a lab assembly or a closely related species, depending on the project.






Note



The choice of reference affects the interpretation of RNA-seq results. Always record which genome and annotation files were used.

title: File Types and File Sizes
text:
5 Pipeline outputs
nf-core pipelines create organized output folders. The exact files depend on the options you choose, but common outputs include:

Quality-control reports
Quantification tables
Alignment files
Pipeline logs
Software version files
MultiQC summary reports

The most useful output to open first is usually:
multiqc_report.html

title: File Types and File Sizes
text:
6 Intermediate files
RNA-seq pipelines also create intermediate files while they are running.
Intermediate files are files created between the raw input files and the final results. They are useful for the pipeline, but they are not always files you need to inspect directly.
One common example is the Nextflow work/ directory. This directory can become large because it stores temporary files for many pipeline steps.






Note



For now, just know that intermediate files can take up space. Later pages will show how to check file sizes and decide what can be cleaned up.

title: File Types and File Sizes
text:
7 Typical storage needs
Exact storage needs depend on the number of samples, read depth, reference files, and pipeline options.
As a rough guide:



Project size
Input FASTQs
Suggested scratch space




Small test run
Less than 5 GB
30 GB


Small project
10-50 GB
100-300 GB


Medium project
50-200 GB
300 GB-1 TB


Large project
More than 200 GB
1 TB or more



For this tutorial, we create a workspace with 30 GB because it is meant for a small demo.

title: File Types and File Sizes
text:
8 What files are most important?
Usually keep:

samplesheet.csv
Final results folder
MultiQC report
Count or expression tables
Pipeline information files
Exact commands and parameters used

Usually do not keep forever:

Large temporary work/ files
Failed test outputs
Duplicate downloaded references
Old intermediate files that can be regenerated

title: File Types and File Sizes
text:
9 Big picture

Raw FASTQ files are the original sequencing data.
Reference files tell the pipeline what genome or annotation to use.
Output files are the results and reports from the pipeline.
Intermediate files help the pipeline run but may be large.
Metadata and notes make the analysis reproducible.







Tip



When in doubt, do not delete raw data, metadata, or final results. Temporary and intermediate files are easier to regenerate than original data.

title: 1 EGAPx instructions for Staurois parvus
text:
These notes document the EGAPx annotation workflow used for the new Staurois parvus genome assembly. They are meant as a practical template for rerunning EGAPx on Unity or adapting the run to another HPC.
Main run scripts:

Initial EGAPx run:
https://github.com/katarinafloer/SparvusGenome/blob/main/run_sparvus_egapx.sbatch
Resume script after the first run hit an out-of-memory error:
https://github.com/katarinafloer/SparvusGenome/blob/main/resume_sparvus_egapx.sbatch
EGAPx config snapshot:
https://github.com/katarinafloer/SparvusGenome/tree/main/egapx_config

Important note: the two SLURM scripts are not the entire setup. EGAPx also needs an input YAML, an RNA-seq manifest, the EGAPx repo/venv, Nextflow + Apptainer/Singularity, and cluster-specific config edits.


For this run, I used:
PROJECT=/scratch3/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-simple/egapx_sparvus
Create the project directory structure:
mkdir -p "$PROJECT"/{input,work,output,container_cache,tmp,logs}



cd "$PROJECT"

git clone https://github.com/ncbi/egapx.git
cd "$PROJECT/egapx"

python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

python ui/egapx.py -V
git rev-parse HEAD | tee "$PROJECT/egapx_commit.txt"
For my run:
EGAPx 0.5.2
commit: 40ec7362576e4b93fa9c5bf0a6c400d9502b8a63



On Unity, I used:
module purge
module load apptainer/latest
module load nextflow/24.04.3
Python 3.12 was available on the system even though module load python/3.12 did not work.
Check versions:
python3 --version
java -version
nextflow -version
apptainer --version
command -v singularity || command -v apptainer



The input YAML was:

text:
4 List files
List files in the current directory:
ls
Show more information, including file sizes:
ls -lh
Example output:
-rw-r--r--  1 user  group   2.1K Jun  8 samplesheet.csv
drwxr-xr-x  4 user  group   128B Jun  8 results






Note



The columns in ls -lh output have specific meanings. In -rw-r--r--  1 user  group   2.1K Jun  8 samplesheet.csv, the first column shows file permissions. -rw-r--r-- means this is a regular file. The owner can read and write it (rw-), the group can read it (r--), and everyone else can read it (r--). A directory usually starts with d, such as drwxr-xr-x. The 1 is the number of links to the file, user is the owner, group is the group, 2.1K is the file size, Jun 8 is the last modified date, and samplesheet.csv is the file name.

title: Using Unity
text:
2 Login nodes
When you first connect to Unity with SSH, you land on a login node.
Your prompt may look like this:
(base) kfloer_smith_edu@login1:~$
Login nodes are for light work, such as:

Navigating directories
Editing small text files
Checking file names
Submitting jobs
Looking at small log files

Do not run large RNA-seq pipelines directly on a login node.






Warning



If a command will use lots of CPU, memory, or disk for more than a few seconds, it probably should not run on the login node.

title: Using Unity
text:
3 Interactive jobs
An interactive job gives you a temporary compute session where you can run commands directly.
Interactive jobs are useful for:

Testing commands
Running small demos
Debugging a pipeline
Checking that software loads correctly
Trying a short nf-core test run

In an interactive job, you still type commands yourself, but the commands run on a compute node instead of the login node.

Note



Interactive jobs are good for learning and testing. They are not always the best choice for long production runs.

title: Using Unity

4 Compute jobs
A compute job is a job submitted to the cluster scheduler. Instead of typing commands one by one, you write a job script and submit it.
Compute jobs are useful for:

Full RNA-seq pipeline runs
Long analyses
Analyses that need many CPUs
Analyses that need lots of memory
Work that should keep running after you log out

A compute job usually includes:

title: Run the Pipeline
text: On Unity, the pipeline runs as a SLURM batch job — not interactively in the terminal. You write a shell script with #SBATCH settings at the top, then submit it with sbatch.

title: Run the Pipeline
text:
1 Run a test first
Before running with your own data, submit a test job to confirm Nextflow, Apptainer, and your workspace are all working.
Save the following as nfcore-rnaseq-test.sh in your home directory. Update the --output, --error, --mail-user, and SCRATCH_RNASEQ lines to match your username and workspace path.
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=nfcore-rnaseq-test
#SBATCH --partition=cpu
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=48G
#SBATCH --time=24:00:00
#SBATCH --output=/home/YOUR_USERNAME/rnaseq_nf_core/job-logs/nfcore-rnaseq-test.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=/home/YOUR_USERNAME/rnaseq_nf_core/job-logs/nfcore-rnaseq-test.%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@email.edu

set -euo pipefail

SCRATCH_RNASEQ=/scratch4/workspace/YOUR_USERNAME-YOUR_WORKSPACE

cd "$SCRATCH_RNASEQ"

module purge
module load nextflow/26.04.1
module load apptainer/latest

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/build-cache"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/tmp"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.nextflow-apptainer-cache"

export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/build-cache"
export APPTAINER_TMPDIR="$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/tmp"
export NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.nextflow-apptainer-cache"
export NXF_OPTS='-Xms1g -Xmx4g'
export PROOT_NO_SECCOMP=1

# Clean up any partial container pulls from a previous attempt
find "$NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR" -type f -name "*.pulling.*" -delete || true

nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq \
  -r 3.26.0 \
  -profile test,unity \
  --outdir test_results \
  -resume
Create the log directory and submit:
mkdir -p ~/rnaseq_nf_core/job-logs
sbatch nfcore-rnaseq-test.sh
Watch progress with:
squeue --me
And check the output log once it starts:
tail -f ~/rnaseq_nf_core/job-logs/nfcore-rnaseq-test.*.out






Tip



The test profile uses a small built-in dataset and finishes in a few hours. If it completes without errors, your environment is ready.

title: Run the Pipeline
text:
2 Run with your own samples
For a real run you need:

A samplesheet CSV listing your samples
A genome FASTA and GTF annotation file
A params JSON file pointing to all of the above


2.1 The samplesheet
The samplesheet must have these four columns:
sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness
C45-1B,/path/to/C45-1B_R1_001.fastq.gz,/path/to/C45-1B_R2_001.fastq.gz,reverse
C45-1H,/path/to/C45-1H_R1_001.fastq.gz,/path/to/C45-1H_R2_001.fastq.gz,reverse
Set strandedness to reverse, forward, or unstranded to match your library prep kit. If you are unsure, check the kit documentation or use the nf-core/rnaseq --salmon_quant_libtype A option to detect it automatically.


2.2 The params file
Rather than putting all options on the command line, save them in a JSON file. Example params.json:
{
  "input": "/path/to/samplesheet.csv",
  "outdir": "/path/to/results",
  "fasta": "/path/to/genome.fna",
  "gtf": "/path/to/annotation.gtf",
  "igenomes_ignore": true,
  "aligner": "star_salmon",
  "pseudo_aligner": "salmon",
  "gtf_extra_attributes": "gene",
  "featurecounts_group_type": "transcript_biotype",
  "max_cpus": 48,
  "max_memory": "256.GB",
  "max_time": "72.h"
}


2.3 The SLURM script
Save the following as run-rnaseq.sh, filling in your paths:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=nfcore-rnaseq
#SBATCH --partition=cpu
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=48G
#SBATCH --time=3-00:00:00
#SBATCH --output=/home/YOUR_USERNAME/rnaseq_nf_core/job-logs/nfcore-rnaseq.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=/home/YOUR_USERNAME/rnaseq_nf_core/job-logs/nfcore-rnaseq.%j.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@email.edu

set -euo pipefail

SCRATCH_RNASEQ=/scratch4/workspace/YOUR_USERNAME-YOUR_WORKSPACE
PARAMS="$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/params.json"

cd "$SCRATCH_RNASEQ"

module purge
module load nextflow/26.04.1
module load apptainer/latest

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/build-cache"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/tmp"

export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/build-cache"
export APPTAINER_TMPDIR="$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/tmp"
export PROOT_TMP_DIR="$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/tmp"
export TMPDIR="$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.apptainer/tmp"
export NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR="$SCRATCH_RNASEQ/.nextflow-apptainer-cache"
export NXF_OPTS='-Xms1g -Xmx4g'
export PROOT_NO_SECCOMP=1

nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq \
  -r 3.26.0 \
  -profile unity \
  -params-file "$PARAMS" \
  -resume
Submit:
sbatch run-rnaseq.sh

3 Resume an interrupted run
Add -resume to your nextflow run command (it is already included in the scripts above). Nextflow caches completed tasks, so resuming picks up from where it stopped without re-running finished steps.






Warning



Only resume with the same params file and the same scratch directory. Changing the output path or key parameters will invalidate the cache.

Keep a copy of your params file and SLURM script alongside your results. The pipeline_info/ folder in your output directory also records the exact parameters, software versions, and execution timeline automatically.

title: Run a Demo Pipeline
text:
Before running an nf-core pipeline, we need a place with enough temporary storage. On Unity, this is called a workspace. A workspace is a scratch directory that gives you more space for data, pipeline outputs, and temporary files.
Workspaces are temporary. The maximum duration is 30 days, but you can extend a workspace if you still need it. When you are finished, you can delete it.
More information: https://docs.unity.rc.umass.edu/documentation/managing-files/hpc-workspace/


Run:
ws_list
Example output:
(base) kfloer_smith_edu@login1:~$ ws_list
id: simple
     workspace directory  : /scratch3/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-simple
     remaining time       : 11 days 7 hours
     creation time        : Wed May 20 18:42:17 2026
     expiration date      : Fri Jun 19 18:42:17 2026
     filesystem name      : workspace
     available extensions : 9998
In this example, I already have one workspace from a different project called simple.



Now create a new workspace called nf-core-demo that will last for 30 days.
Run:
ws_allocate nf-core-demo 30
Example output:
(base) kfloer_smith_edu@login1:~$ ws_allocate nf-core-demo 30
Info: could not read email from users config ~/.ws_user.conf.
Info: reminder email will be sent to local user account
Info: creating workspace.
/scratch4/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-nf-core-demo
remaining extensions  : 10000
remaining time in days: 30
The important line is the workspace path:
/scratch4/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-nf-core-demo
This is the directory we will use for the tutorial.



Run:
ws_list
Example output:
(base) kfloer_smith_edu@login1:~$ ws_list
id: nf-core-demo
     workspace directory  : /scratch4/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-nf-core-demo
     remaining time       : 29 days 23 hours
     creation time        : Mon Jun  8 11:03:16 2026
     expiration date      : Wed Jul  8 11:03:16 2026
     filesystem name      : workspace
     available extensions : 10000

id: simple
     workspace directory  : /scratch3/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-simple
     remaining time       : 11 days 7 hours
     creation time        : Wed May 20 18:42:17 2026
     expiration date      : Fri Jun 19 18:42:17 2026
     filesystem name      : workspace
     available extensions : 9998
Now I have two workspaces:

nf-core-demo, which we just created
simple, from an older project




Run:
cd /scratch4/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-nf-core-demo
Your exact path may be different, so copy the path shown by your own ws_list output.



If your workspace is about to expire but you still need it, you can extend it.
Run:
ws_extend nf-core-demo 30
Example output:
(base) kfloer_smith_edu@login1:~$ ws_extend nf-core-demo 30
Info: extending workspace.
remaining extensions  : 9999
remaining time in days: 30
Check that the expiration date changed:
ws_list
Example output:
id: nf-core-demo
     workspace directory  : /scratch4/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-nf-core-demo
     remaining time       : 29 days 23 hours
     expiration date      : Fri Aug  7 11:03:16 2026
Your exact expiration date will be different.



Only do this when you are completely finished with the tutorial files.
Run:
ws_release nf-core-demo
Then check your workspaces again:
ws_list
Example output:
(base) kfloer_smith_edu@login1:~$ ws_list
id: simple
     workspace directory  : /scratch3/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-simple
     remaining time       : 11 days 7 hours
     creation time        : Wed May 20 18:42:17 2026
     expiration date      : Fri Jun 19 18:42:17 2026
     filesystem name      : workspace
     available extensions : 9998
Now nf-core-demo is gone, and only the older workspace remains.
